edits.old: In 2017 Kristalina Georgieva, then chief executive of the World Bank, went to the home of a manager on the Bank's Doing Business team to collect a printed copy of the final report, and thanked the employee for helping to resolve the problem. That is one detail from an investigation by the law firm WilmerHale, published in September 2021, which found that staff had changed China's data under pressure from the office of the Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, and from Georgieva, at a time when the Bank was seeking China's support for a large increase in its capital. The changes put China at 78th in the 2018 edition, seven places higher than the draft data had it. Georgieva said she disagreed fundamentally with the findings, and the IMF's board, where she had become managing director, backed her in October 2021. Doing Business ranked 190 countries on how easy they made it to start and run a company; investors used it and governments rewrote laws to climb it. The suspicion is that global rankings like this are bent for countries the institution needs or that pay it, and that the scoring itself pushed countries to strip protections from workers.

edits.old: China was not the only case. For the 2020 edition WilmerHale found data changed for three more countries: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan. The first stated consideration in the Saudi change was Jordan, not money. In September 2019 Simeon Djankov, then the Bank's development economics director, told the Doing Business team to find a way to drop Jordan from the top of the draft Top Improvers list, saying the troubles Jordan was in made that ranking not credible. He sent an employee to Jordan, who reported that Jordan's data was correct; the team then looked for ways to lift Saudi Arabia past it. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named top improver, and it had paid the Bank for advisory work on the very indicators being scored. In 2006 Saudi Arabia's king had said he wanted the country among the top ten by 2010. WilmerHale's finding is that the changes were "likely" meant to reward Saudi Arabia for its role at the Bank, and it lists those paid contracts as one of three things that could have motivated the official, not as the cause. The United Arab Emirates' data was changed because its tax system was similar to Saudi Arabia's, and that change did not move its ranking. The Bank cancelled Doing Business.

edits.old: Azerbaijan's data was changed the other way, and no money was in it. Djankov had the team check Azerbaijan's reforms in August 2019; its own internal audit confirmed most of them, and he had three left uncounted anyway, which cut the score by nearly two points and dropped the country off the Top Improvers list. He told the investigators he doubted the reforms were real, and several employees said he appeared to harbour a personal animus against the country. In neither the Saudi nor the Azerbaijan change did WilmerHale find evidence that the president's office or the board was involved. There had been warnings. In January 2018 the Bank's chief economist, Paul Romer, said Chile had fallen in the rankings because of changes in method rather than in Chile, and suggested politics might be behind it. He then said he had not meant to suggest manipulation, and resigned; Augusto Lopez-Claros, who had directed the group that published the rankings, called the claim that the changes targeted Chile wholly without merit. The rankings also shaped laws. Until 2009 they scored countries higher for weaker worker protections, through what was called the employing workers indicator. The Bank suspended that indicator in 2009 after pressure from unions, the International Labour Organization and the US Congress, and an independent panel the Bank set up in 2013 recommended removing it permanently.

edits.old: In July 2004 a US Senate investigations subcommittee reported on Riggs Bank, a Washington bank that held accounts for more than 95 per cent of the foreign embassies in the city. Its single largest customer was the government and ruling family of Equatorial Guinea, a small West African country where oil had been found but most people stayed poor. From 1995 Riggs held more than 60 accounts and certificates of deposit for the government, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema, his relatives and officials. The subcommittee gives the size of that business two ways: aggregate deposits "ranging from $400 to $700 million at a time", and, in its findings, balances and outstanding loans that together approached $700 million by 2003. It found that Riggs had helped set up offshore shell companies for the president and his sons, accepted nearly $13 million in cash deposits into accounts controlled by the president and his wife, some of it carried in by suitcase, and let more than $35 million be wired from government accounts to companies it had reason to think the president controlled. Its finding, under the heading Turning a Blind Eye, is that Riggs serviced these accounts with little or no attention to its anti-money-laundering obligations and turned a blind eye to evidence that it was handling the proceeds of foreign corruption. US regulators fined Riggs $25 million in 2004, and in January 2005 it pleaded guilty to failing to report suspicious transactions and paid a further $16 million. The prosecutor said Riggs had aggressively cultivated the accounts despite repeated warnings. The suspicion is that large Western banks regularly take and move money stolen from the public of poor countries, because it is profitable, and treat the occasional fine as a cost of business.

edits.old: Britain's regulator looked at the same kind of money and found something narrower. After the death in 1998 of General Sani Abacha, whose regime was estimated to have taken at least $5 billion, the Financial Services Authority examined how London banks had handled his family's money. In March 2001 it reported 42 personal and corporate account relationships linked to the Abacha family and close associates at 23 banks, with $1.3 billion of turnover on those accounts between 1996 and 2000, 98 per cent of it at 15 banks with significant weaknesses in their anti-money-laundering controls. What the regulator found was a failure of control rather than knowledge: it said the turnover figure did not necessarily represent proceeds of crime or money received into Britain, it noted that a number of the banks had reported their suspicions to the national criminal intelligence service in good time, and it had no power at that date to name any bank. None of them was prosecuted.

edits.old: In September 2020 the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and BuzzFeed News published the FinCEN Files, more than 2,100 reports that banks had filed with the US Treasury about transactions they suspected. Between 1999 and 2017 the banks had flagged more than $2 trillion in payments, and the leak showed that five global banks, JPMorgan Chase, HSBC, Standard Chartered, Deutsche Bank and Bank of New York Mellon, kept moving money for suspect clients even after being fined for earlier failures. Banks can stop a suspicious payment but often are not required to; filing a report is often enough. A report is not in itself evidence of wrongdoing; the banks denied systematic wrongdoing, and FinCEN, the Treasury agency that receives the reports, condemned the leak.

edits.old: Jakarta's water went the same way earlier. The World Bank lent Jakarta's water company $92 million in 1991 and assigned consultants who advised privatisation. The Bank's own completion report on that loan, dated 23 June 1998, says two things in one sentence: the privatisation of the city water company's operations was an event "parallel to but facilitated by the Project", and it was not envisaged by the government or the Bank when the loan was appraised, because private sector participation was still a new concept at that time. At paragraph 28 the report adds that in the late 1980s, had the government proposed a private-participation option, it would most likely have been turned down by the Bank, after other unsuccessful experiences in Indonesia. The Bank's own account, then, is that its loan helped Jakarta's privatisation along without the Bank having designed or wanted it. In 1997, without open bidding, the city was split between Britain's Thames Water, whose local company gave 20 per cent to President Suharto's son, and France's Suez, partnered with the Salim Group of a Suharto associate. Tariffs rose by 35, 40 and 30 per cent in three years, and coverage reached only 59 per cent by 2015 against a 98 per cent target. In October 2017 Indonesia's Supreme Court found the privatisation had not improved water quality, quantity or continuity and ordered it ended.

what_i_verified: The corroborating paragraph-28 sentence (late 1980s, a private-participation option would most likely have been turned down by the Bank) is the only thing cut. The correction it corroborated is intact: the completion report of 23 June 1998 still carries both halves of its own sentence, 'parallel to but facilitated by the Project' and not envisaged by the government or the Bank at appraisal because private sector participation was a new concept then.

For the apparent contradiction, I opened the entry's own ICIJ source (Andreas Harsono, Water and politics in the fall of Suharto). It says: 'Both organizations were encouraging Indonesia at the time to privatize its utilities, according to World Bank loan documents. The World Bank expected that the loans would facilitate privatization by bolstering the water and sewage infrastructure, making the waterworks a more attractive investment. The World Bank also appointed consultants to advise PAM Jaya on the privatization.'

So the joining sentence rests on a source already on the card: the Bank was encouraging privatisation and expected this loan to make the waterworks a more attractive investment (ICIJ, from Bank loan documents), while its own completion report says the particular handover was not envisaged at appraisal. Neither half is dropped, and no new source is needed.
The one quote from the completion report is unchanged and still the entry's only quote from it.

edits.old: The record goes back decades. In the early 1960s the US aid agency set up a public safety programme to train foreign police, run mostly through its Office of Public Safety, and a General Accounting Office report released to the Senate by Senator Alan Cranston on 5 March 1992 sets out what it grew into: by 1968 the United States was spending $60 million a year training police in 34 countries, in subjects that included interrogation, riot control and counterinsurgency techniques, and also supplying weapons and communications equipment. Introducing the report, Cranston listed among its flaws that US intelligence agencies were given an important role in developing and running the programmes, and said Congress banned foreign aid to police forces in 1974 after reports that US-trained police in Iran, Vietnam and Brazil were involved in torture, murder and the suppression of political activity. The same report records five US departments training police from 125 countries in fiscal 1990 at a cost of about $117 million. Forty years later, in 2014, the Associated Press revealed that USAID had built ZunZuneo, a text-message network for Cubans, through front companies in Spain and the Cayman Islands, paid through foreign banks. By USAID's own count it had about 68,000 users before it shut down in September 2012, and they were not told who had made it. USAID said the programme was not covert.

Uruguay and Brazil: I opened the National Security Archive's Electronic Briefing Book 324 (To Save Dan Mitrione, 11 August 2010). It states that Dan Mitrione was 'Director of the U.S. AID Office of Public Safety (OPS) in Uruguay and the main American advisor to the Uruguayan police at the time', that he was found dead on 10 August 1970 after ten days held by MLN-Tupamaro insurgents, that 'The U.S. AID Office of Public Safety helped enhance the counterinsurgency techniques of a Uruguayan police renowned for the wide use of torture among prisoners' and that under him the OPS consolidated the police's DNII, and that 'In the mid 1960's, he was hired by the U.S. AID Office of Public Safety to train policemen in Brazil and Uruguay.' It does not give 1964 or any start year for the Uruguay programme, so the 'from 1964' in the live note is not re-sourced and is dropped.

Guatemala: I opened the Guatemalan National Police Historical Archive's own report, Del Silencio a la Memoria, volume 1, chapter II (hosted by Equipo Nizkor). It states that declassified US documents record the Public Safety Program in Guatemala (PSP) beginning in 1956 on the basis of Fred G. Fimbres's 9 April 1956 report for USAID's International Cooperation Administration; that coordination between Guatemala's security forces in the 1960s came about with the advice of USAID's Office of Public Safety; that USAID's chief public safety adviser for the region, John P. Longan, was in Guatemala from 27 November to 7 December 1965; and it cites USAID's own 'Analisis de cinco anos: Programa de Seguridad Publica-Guatemala 1967-1971', including the training of 63 officers who then took key posts in the National Police and the Guardia de Hacienda. Nothing in it, or in anything else I opened, calls Guatemala's the largest Office of Public Safety programme in Central America.

Note for the record, not a card change: the AHPN report dates Guatemala's Public Safety Program to 1956, before the Office of Public Safety itself existed; the card's 'In the early 1960s the US aid agency set up a public safety programme ... run mostly through its Office of Public Safety' is about the agency-wide programme and the GAO item behind it, so the two do not conflict, but the Guatemala note should not imply OPS was there from 1956.
